title: Why does the share table refresh twice on boot
text: Letting the first tick do it means the process serves requests for up to one interval with an empty table, which for a 30 second refresh is 30 seconds of falling back to FIFO on every deploy. Keep the eager refresh, await it before the server listens, and start the interval after.

title: Reading deadlock counts after a deploy
text: `pg_stat_database` gives you a cumulative `deadlocks` count per database along with `stats_reset`, so the query is the count now minus the count you recorded before, and you should read `stats_reset` in the same query to know the baseline is still valid. It survives a client restart but not `pg_stat_reset()`, and on a crash-and-recover the counters can be discarded. For a deploy window the practical approach is to snapshot the row immediately before, since the absolute number since the beginning of time is not interesting and the delta is.

title: Asserting a lock order in a test
text: Query pg_locks from a third connection while the transaction under test is paused between its two acquisitions: the rows carry relation, mode and granted, and the order they appear in by `pid` and grant time is the order the path took them. That is a real assertion rather than an absence-of-failure one, and it fails loudly if someone reorders the statements. Keep the pause behind a test-only hook so production has no barrier in it, and assert on relation oids resolved by name so a table rename does not silently turn the test into a no-op.

title: A deadlock test that fails every run
text: Drive the interleaving from the test rather than hoping for it. Open both transactions, have each take its first lock and then await a barrier the test controls, release the barrier, and only then let each take its second. Both second locks are now guaranteed to be requested while the other is held. Set deadlock_timeout low on the test connections so the detector fires in tens of milliseconds instead of a second, and assert on SQLSTATE 40P01 rather than on the message text.

title: Staging soak, 60 orgs
text: Watch `pg_stat_database.deadlocks` before and after - if it does not move at all, the soak is not producing contention and a green run means nothing. Watch lock wait time, either from `pg_stat_activity` sampled for wait_event_type = 'Lock' or from log_lock_waits with deadlock_timeout set low, because waits without deadlocks is the signal that the ordering fix is working rather than that the contention disappeared. And watch renewals that gave up: zero deadlocks with a rising give-up count means you moved the failure rather than removed it.

title: SET, SET LOCAL and search_path in a pooled connection
text: Move them inside the transaction as SET LOCAL, which reverts at commit and therefore cannot leak into the next client that gets the connection. For values that genuinely must apply to every session, set them on the role with ALTER ROLE ... SET, so Postgres applies them at backend start and the pooler never has to carry them. The one to be careful with is search_path: a leaked search_path is a security problem rather than a correctness one, because the next tenant's unqualified names resolve somewhere they should not.

title: Where auditlog.ts decides what to record
text: The decision is the AUDITED_RESOURCES list at the top of auditlog.ts, applied by the router middleware rather than by the handlers, so a route is audited by appearing in that list and by nothing else. A new route gets nothing by default: it is not in the list, so it writes no entry, and there is no warning anywhere. The list is typed against the resource union, so adding a resource name that does not exist fails at build - but omitting a route entirely is invisible.

title: Reading the Go toolchain version at build time
text: runtime.Version() gives you the toolchain that built the running binary, which is not the same thing as the toolchain that will build the customer's code - for a cache key you want the latter, and it only exists where the build actually runs. The usual shape is for the runner to report it as part of the build environment and for the key to hash what it was told, so the cache service never guesses. debug.ReadBuildInfo() gives you the same for the current binary plus module versions, which is useful for your own telemetry and still not the answer for the key.

title: Property tests over a concurrency limiter
text: Four carry most of the value: held never exceeds the limit, held never goes negative, release is idempotent for a given identity, and after any sequence of operations that ends with every lease terminal the count is exactly zero. The last one catches leaks, which is the failure you actually have, and it is the one people leave out because it needs the generator to drain rather than stop at a random point. Generate interleavings of acquire, renew, expire and reclaim rather than acquire and release only.

title: Deterministic timing in a soak test
text: It means something about ordering and nothing about contention. Fake timers will faithfully reproduce which org is selected in which round, which is where Monday's bug lived, but they remove every effect that comes from work taking real time - lock hold, event loop lag, a refresh landing mid-selection. Keep the fake-timer version as the fast test that runs on every pull request, and keep one real-time run for the things fake timers erase.

title: bigint or a decimal library in TypeScript
text: If every amount is an integer number of minor units then bigint is enough and has no dependency, no configuration and no chance of two call sites using different rounding modes. The catch is JSON: bigint does not serialise, so send it as a string and parse it at the edge, which is a good habit anyway because a JSON number over 2^53 is silently wrong. Reach for a decimal library only when you genuinely need fractional minor units, such as unit prices quoted to four places - carrying it for totals alone is a dependency buying you nothing.

title: Why this handler can send 200 and then nothing
text: The handler sets the status and content-type immediately after resolving the key, before the S3 GET returns a single byte, so the response is committed while the upstream call is still outstanding. When that read times out mid-stream the only remaining option is to close the body, which the client sees as a complete zero-length 200. Deferring the header until the first byte arrives is what makes a 504 possible at all.

title: Testing that a code path touches no backend
text: Construct the handler with clients that throw on any method call, then drive the shed path and assert it returns normally - the test passes only if nothing reached them. This is stronger than mocking with recorded calls because it fails on the first unexpected access rather than on an assertion at the end, and the failure message points at the line that broke the property. Name the test after the property rather than the function, so the next person understands they are being told not to do something.

text: Put a version number on the membership row and make it part of the cache key: a revoke increments the version, every cached entry under the old key becomes unreachable, and you have invalidated exactly one subject without touching anyone else's entries. title: Reviewing a batched delete for exactly-once
text: Committed batches stay deleted and the manifest never records them, so a rerun re-scans keys that are already gone - harmless for a delete, but the manifest then understates what the run removed, which is the artefact you keep for exactly this situation. The cursor is opened inside each batch's transaction and the key range is derived from the previous batch's last key, so a restart resumes from the manifest rather than from zero only if the manifest is written per batch, not at the end. As written, a crash at batch 400 of 500 loses the record of 400 batches.

title: What the refill path in warm.go does today
text: The ticker fires every 30 seconds and tops the pool back up to its target, so a claim does not itself start a replacement - it just removes a machine and waits for the next tick. The buffered channel serialises launches so two ticks cannot both launch, which means the effective refill rate is one machine per tick regardless of how many are missing. Under a burst that drains the pool, recovery is therefore linear in ticks and the pool stays empty for most of the burst.

title: Retention windows for audit logs
text: The framework does not name a number - it asks you to define a period and then show you honour it, so a documented 90 days you actually enforce passes where an undocumented forever does not. In practice the number is set by whatever else already binds you: contractual commitments to customers, any regulated data in the log, and the length of the audit period itself, which means you need at least the full observation window plus the time to complete the audit. The failure mode auditors find is not a short retention, it is a policy that says one thing and a table that says another.

The two things that usually go wrong are verifying over a re-marshalled struct, which changes key order and whitespace and fails for no visible reason, and reading the signature file as text so a trailing newline ends up in the signature. title: Read this plan file format and tell me what breaks
text: There is no version discriminator, so a newer writer and an older reader produce a successful run over zero tests: the reader finds no key it recognises, iterates an empty list, and exits zero. The reader also falls back to running the whole suite when parsing fails, which means a malformed plan looks like a slow but passing build rather than an error. Both failures are silent and both are green, which is the worst combination for something whose entire purpose is to run a subset - add a version field, fail closed on anything you do not understand, and make the exit code distinguishable from a test failure.

text: The client treats a clean close at timeout as a normal empty response and reconnects immediately, so behaviour is correct, but the reconnect has no jitter: every watcher that started within the same second will return within the same second forever. There is also no cap on consecutive empty responses, so a route that is broken in a way that returns 200 with no body turns into a tight reconnect loop rather than a visible error. title: What changed in lease.ts since yesterday
text: Renewal was a single UPDATE on the lease row; it is now a transaction that reads the org's contract FOR UPDATE, counts unexpired leases for that org, then extends or refuses. The count filters on expiry rather than on the row existing, so a lagging sweeper no longer makes an org look over its limit. A refusal calls into queue.ts to requeue at the head of the org's queue - the only place this branch touches the queue - and refusals carry limit_source so they are countable separately from expiries.

title: Deploying a schema change and its writer together
text: Adding a nullable column is backwards compatible, so run the migration first and deploy the writer after - old instances ignore a column they do not know about, and the reverse order gives you a window where the writer fails on every request. The rule that generalises is that expanding changes go before the code and contracting changes go after it, with a release in between where both shapes are valid. It is only the same deploy when you are willing to have the migration and the rollout succeed or fail together, which for a write path in the request cycle you are not.

title: Reading the refill path in warm.go
text: Claims five to ten fall through to the normal launch path and pay the full cold start, because nothing starts a replacement until the first of those jobs finishes and calls release. The refill is therefore driven by job duration rather than by pool size, so the pool recovers slowest exactly when demand is highest. A loop that watches the count and launches toward the floor decouples the two.

title: Keying duration history through a rename
text: A content hash identifies a pure rename and nothing else, and in a real refactor the file is usually renamed and edited in the same commit, so the hash changes too. The options that actually survive that are similarity matching, as git does for rename detection, or reading the rename from version control directly if the plan has access to it. Both are more machinery than the problem usually justifies - one bad day of shard balance is often cheaper than a heuristic that is confidently wrong on a different day.

title: Typing a route's declared resource in TypeScript
text: Make the registration function take the resource as a required parameter rather than reading it off the handler. If routes are registered through one helper whose signature is `(method, path, resource: Resource, handler)`, omitting it is a type error at the call site and there is nowhere to forget it. A union type for Resource then gives you exhaustiveness on the audited set, so adding a resource without deciding whether it is audited also fails to compile.

title: Does Retry-After leak anything between tenants
text: Only if the bucket you read is not the bucket that rejected the request - for instance if a shared route-level limiter runs before the per-org one and you report its reset. Then the value is a function of global traffic and a determined caller can infer load from other tenants by sampling it. The fix is structural rather than a check: return the reset of whichever limiter produced the rejection, and have the limiter return the value with the decision instead of looking it up afterwards.

title: What an EC2 warm pool actually guarantees
text: A warm pool gives you pre-initialised instances in a stopped or running state that scale-out draws from before launching new ones, so the guarantee is only that a hit is fast, never that there will be a hit. Refill is asynchronous and bounded by instance launch and initialisation time, typically a minute or more, so a burst arriving faster than refill drains the pool and every subsequent request pays the full cold path. The practical consequence is that pool size has to be chosen against burst arrival rate rather than average demand, and the hit rate is the number worth measuring.

title: Is a lockfile enough to identify a build environment
text: No. A lockfile pins the dependency graph, which is one input among several. It says nothing about the compiler, the standard library shipped with it, the linker, the libc, or the build flags, all of which change the output bytes. Treat the lockfile as necessary and nowhere near sufficient.

title: Retention that is a job and not a sentence
text: Partition the table by month and drop whole partitions, rather than running a delete over a large table on a schedule. A drop is instant and takes no locks anyone will notice, while a bulk delete of a year's rows bloats the table and competes with the writes you care about. Export the age of the oldest partition as a metric so that the policy being true is something you can see on a dashboard, which is also what an auditor will ask you to demonstrate.

title: Properties worth asserting for an admission policy
text: Three that the fairness tests cannot see. place: infra
title: Advisory locks under transaction pooling
text: It breaks silently, which is the dangerous part. In transaction mode a client is assigned a server connection for the duration of a transaction and then loses it, so a session-level advisory lock is left held on a server connection your client no longer owns and will be handed to someone else. The lock is never released until that server connection is closed, and your next call to take it may land on a different server connection and succeed - so two clients both believe they hold it. Either use pg_advisory_xact_lock, which is released at commit and is safe in transaction mode, or put that service on a session-mode pool.

title: Counting concurrency by claim or by lease
text: The slot leaks. A reclaim creates a second claim for the same unit of work, and if only the finishing path releases, the first claim's slot is held until the process restarts. title: Why the retry made it worse
text: Because the retry recreates the conditions for the next deadlock rather than waiting for them to clear. The killed transaction restarts immediately into the same contention, and meanwhile the work it was protecting - the lease renewal - did not happen, so the lease expires, the job is reclaimed and admission runs again, which adds another contender. That is a livelock: progress is zero even though every participant is behaving correctly and no one is blocked. Unbounded retry without backoff or a budget is the usual way to build one, and the symptom is exactly what you saw - high CPU, no errors that look fatal, and throughput of nothing.

title: PAUSE semantics during a cutover
text: PAUSE waits for all current transactions to finish, then holds every server connection closed while clients stay connected and simply block on their next query. title: Recovery curve after a full cache invalidation
text: It falls to near zero within one build cycle, then recovers along the distribution of your repeat traffic rather than linearly: the first day recovers whatever share of builds repeat daily, which is usually the largest single group, and the tail takes as long as your least frequent recurring build. title: Two transactions touching the same two tables
text: You get a deadlock when two transactions take the same locks in different orders, so the fix is to make every path take them in one order and to write that order somewhere a reader will find it.
